Many stress that the punishment of the hereafter is greater, and that these people repented.

This passage tells of the owners of a garden near Sanaa who resolved to deny the poor their share of its produce. A calamity from God struck the garden by night while they slept, and it was left black as the darkness of night. The commentators interpret the word tâ'if differently: al-Tabari and Ibn 'Abbas take it as a command or decree from God, Qatada as a punishment, and Ibn Jurayj as a tongue of fire from the valley of hell, while al-Farra' holds that the word refers only to something that comes at night. As for sarim, al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir explain it as the black night or black ash, al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Ashur as a land stripped bare, and al-Hasan as a garden emptied of its good. Most commentators agree that the offence was the intention to deprive the poor, compounded by the omission of "if God wills" in their oath. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Zamakhshari report that the owners repented, and Mujahid says they were given a better garden in return. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir present the story as an example for the Quraysh, who were tested with famine after rejecting their Prophet, and all who discuss it agree that the punishment of the Hereafter is greater.

This verse describes the garden whose owners swore to harvest its fruit at dawn and deny the poor any share. A calamity sent by God struck it by night while they slept, and the garden was left burnt and ruined. The commentators agree that the tā'if was a trial or command from God, but they differ on its nature. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Juraij and others describe it as a fire sent from heaven or a tongue of fire, Qatada speaks simply of a punishment, and al-Farra' holds that a tā'if only comes at night. On the word ṣarīm, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Farra' give it the sense of black ash or the dark night, al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Thawri take it to mean something cut off, that is a harvested field stripped of its produce, while al-Mu'arrij understands a dune cut off from the rest of the sand. All agree that the owners intended to deprive the poor, that their punishment matched their intention, and that the most upright among them reminded them to say 'if God wills'. Reports transmitted through Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid add that they repented and God gave them a better garden. The verse was cited as a warning to the Quraysh, who were tested with famine after prosperity. Accounts differ on the location of the garden, between Yemen, Sanaa, Ṣawrān or Ḍarawān, and on whether its owners were Jews, Abyssinians or People of the Book.

This verse describes the people of the garden who, at morning, called out to one another to set off early to their orchard and harvest its fruit, if they were determined to do so. The commentators explain that the calling out means urging one another to set off at the appointed time, that setting out early means leaving at dawn, that the tilth refers to the fruit, crops and vines, and that cutting means harvesting. They agree that these people had secretly resolved to deny the poor, so they spoke in lowered voices so no one would hear, saying to one another that no needy person should enter their garden that day. The phrase rendered as going out early with a fixed intention, able to do so has been read in several ways. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd take it to mean capability or determination, Mujahid and al-Hasan take it as haste or need, Sufyan and al-Suddi as anger, Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn Qutayba as refusal to give, and some as the name of the garden or village. Al-Zamakhshari takes it to mean that they were able in their own estimation, and Ibn Kathir similarly holds that they thought themselves capable. Most commentators understand the exception that they omitted to be saying if God wills, while Mujahid and Abu Salih take it to be saying glory be to God. They also agree that the garden was destroyed by fire or a punishment from heaven, and that its owners repented, and God gave them something better in return.

This verse records the call the people of the garden make to one another at dawn, urging each other to go early to their field and cut the fruit, if they are determined to do so. The commentators agree that the aim is to spur them to leave promptly and carry out their plan, and that the words carry a hint of their intention to deny the poor. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the verb "harvesting" means cutting the produce, while Ibn Atiyya notes that the word may also mean being resolute. Al-Zamakhshari explains that "upon" is used because going out to cut the crop amounts to going upon it, or because the verb carries the sense of setting out towards it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir speak of the field as a crop in general, while Mujahid and Ibn Juzayy mention grapes or fruit in particular. The commentators link the verse to the full story: the children of a pious man inherited the garden, resolved to withhold the poor's share, were punished by the destruction of their orchard, and then repented. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur present the parable as a warning to the Quraysh, who ignored God's blessings as those people did.

This verse describes the people of the garden setting out to their orchard while speaking in low voices to one another, lest anyone overhear and the poor come to them. The commentators agree that the verb means speaking secretly and in a hushed tone, and that their whispered words were that no needy person should enter their garden that day. Ibn Abbas adds that they set out while it was still dark. Al-Zamakhshari explains that they lowered their voices for fear the needy would notice them, whereas al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Farra' understand it as conferring among themselves. The word hard in the following verse has been read in several ways. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Mujahid take it to mean determination and purpose, Abu Ubayda and al-Qutaybi take it to mean withholding, al-Sudi and Sufyan take it to mean anger and resentment, and Ibn Abbas takes it to mean power. Al-Tabari prefers the sense of a settled intention, without claiming certainty. Al-Zamakhshari notes that their going out was to harvest the fruit, which explains the use of the preposition 'ala'. Ibn Atiyya reports that the whispering was out of fear that the poor would sense them. The majority conclude that they were punished by the loss of their garden and then repented.

This passage tells of the owners of the garden who swore to harvest their fruit at dawn, secretly from the poor, saying that no needy person should enter that day, and set off early, believing they had the means. The commentators agree on the plain sense: they intended to deny the poor a share their father had long given, and God punished them by striking the garden during the night, so that it became black like night or burned. Ibn Abbas and Qatada say the tha'if was a punishment or command from God, Ibn Juraij says it was a tongue of fire, and others say it was a command from God.

Scholars differ on the meaning of "hard". Al-Hasan, Qatada, Mujahid and Abu al-Aliya take it as resolve and haste; 'Ikrima, al-Sha'bi, al-Suddi and Sufyan take it as anger toward the poor; Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn Qutayba take it as withholding, as a she-camel or the year is said to withhold its milk or rain; Ibn Abbas takes it as ability. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba read "capable" as having settled their plan or being able to carry it out.

All agree that the most sensible among them, Awsatuhum, rebuked them for not saying "if God wills" or for not glorifying God. Mujahid and Abu Salih take their exception as "Glory be to God". Others read it as "why do you not glorify God and thank Him?". They then acknowledged their wrong and asked God for something better; according to Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid, God gave them a better garden. Ibn Kathir concludes that the parable applies to the Quraysh who rejected the blessing of the Prophet's mission.

This passage describes the owners of the garden setting out at dawn, determined to harvest its fruit and deny the poor their share, and confident they had the power to do so. The commentators differ over the meaning of the word hardin. Mujahid, Qatada, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd take it to mean determination and firm resolve, that they had agreed on a plan among themselves. Al-Sha'bi, Sufyan and al-Suddi understand it as anger and rage, citing a verse of al-Ashhab ibn Rumayla. Abu 'Ubayda, Ibn Qutayba and Ibn al-Jawzi render it as withholding, as when a year is dry of rain or a she-camel gives no milk. Al-Hasan also gives the sense of poverty, Ibn 'Abbas that of capability, and al-Suddi says it is the name of the garden or the village. Most read their being capable as meaning that they believed they were able to harvest. Al-Farra' and al-Zamakhshari also admit the sense of restricting the poor's portion. When they saw the garden blackened, they thought they had lost their way, then recognised it and admitted they were deprived because of their intention. Commentators agree that the story is a parable for the Quraysh, tested first with abundance and then with hardship, and they note the repentance of the owners who acknowledged their wrong and hoped for something better. According to Ibn 'Atiyya and others, the fault lay not only in refusing the poor but also in omitting the exception "if God wills", which some equate with glorifying God. Abu Salih and Mujahid link that exception to glorification, while others take it as seeking forgiveness.

This verse describes the people of the garden when they arrive and see their orchard burnt black and bare. At first they do not recognise it and think they have lost their way. Al-Tabari, Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir present this as a spontaneous reaction of surprise, and they recognise the garden only after looking closely. Qatada takes it to mean that they really took a wrong path, whereas al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi see it as a fault of intention, since they had planned to deprive the poor. Once they recognise the garden, they say they have been deprived of its produce. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi report that their most upright brother reproached them for not saying "if God wills". Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir agree, as do Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj. Abu Salih and others take the glorification to mean the exception itself, while some understand it as prayer, seeking forgiveness or thanking God. Zamakhshari holds that the rebuke concerns both the refusal to help the poor and the omission of the exception. When they confess their wrong with "Glory be to our Lord", they blame one another, then ask God for something better than the garden. Commentators such as Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid report that God gave them a better garden. In its context, the story is a warning to the Quraysh, urging them to repent before punishment reaches them.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the moment when the people of the garden reached their orchard and found it burned and stripped of its fruit. At first they thought they had lost their way, and one of them said, "Indeed we are lost." Then, looking more carefully and recognising it as their own, they said, "Rather, we are deprived," meaning they had lost its produce because of their intention to deny the poor. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi all record this reading. The phrase "awsatuhum" is understood by Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid as the most just or the best of them, and it is he who rebuked them for not saying "if God wills." Ibn Juzayy and Ibn al-Jawzi, following the majority, take the glorification to mean that exception, while Abu Salih holds that their exception was simply saying "Glory be to God," and others take it to mean thanking or seeking forgiveness. Scholars differ on the meaning of "harad": Ibn Abbas and Qatada give determination or haste, Abu Ubayda gives withholding, and al-Suddi gives anger. Al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report that they then repented, saying "Glory be to our Lord, we were wrongdoers," and hoped for something better from God, and Ibn Jurayj and al-Baghawi mention that a better garden was granted. Ibn Kathir adds that the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, and Ibn Sa'di sees the worldly loss as a warning to those who deny.

This verse records the words of the most just and wisest among the owners of the garden, who rebukes them for not saying "if God wills". The commentators first explain the situation: when they saw their garden burnt and its fruit gone, they at first thought they had lost their way, then realised it was their own garden and that they were deprived of its produce, having planned to withhold it from the poor. The phrase "tusabbihun" is taken by most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, to mean the exception clause "in sha Allah"; Mujahid and Abu Salih specify that their exception was the formula "subhan Allah". Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari justify this naming on the ground that the phrase affirms that nothing happens without God's will. Others read the term as remembrance of God, thanks for His blessings, or repentance, and al-Hasan takes it to mean prayer. Ibn Juzayy and al-Nasafi note that the man had urged them to this course in vain. After confessing their wrong, they blame one another, repent and hope for something better. These scholars apply the story to the Quraysh, struck by famine, and stress that the punishment of the Hereafter is greater.

This verse records the words of the people of the garden after their orchard was destroyed: Glory be to our Lord, we were indeed wrongdoers. They declare God free of injustice and admit their own wrong, namely denying the poor their share of the fruit and failing to say "if God wills" in their oath. The commentators generally agree that they repented, blamed one another, and hoped their Lord would give them something better in place of their garden. Many, including al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, read the story as a parable for the Quraysh, who were tested with famine. They differ on the meaning of the glorification. Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj, followed by most, take it to mean the exception "if God wills"; Abu Salih takes it as simply saying "glory be to God"; al-Hasan takes it as prayer; al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi see it as a glorification that combines the exception with declaring God's absolute power. On the word "harad", Ibn Abbas says capability, Qatada determination, al-Sudi and al-Sha'bi anger, and Abu Ubayda withholding. Ibn Mas'ud reports that they were given a better garden, while al-Hasan questioned whether their words showed true faith.

This passage describes the reaction of the people of the garden after they find their orchard destroyed. Some turn toward others and blame one another, each shifting responsibility onto his companions for the plan to deny the poor their share. Commentators explain that this mutual blame concerned their resolve to withhold what was owed to the needy: some had proposed it, some approved, some kept silent in acceptance, and some rejected it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that their eldest had reminded them to glorify God and to say "if God wills," but they did not heed him. Scholars differ on what the istithna' (the exception) means: most take it as the phrase "if God wills," Abu Salih and Mujahid as the glorification "Glory be to God," and al-Hasan as the prayer, while al-Zamakhshari links the two because both exalt God. They then admit that they were wrongdoers and had gone beyond the limits, and they hope that God will give them something better than the garden. Ibn Mas'ud reports that they were sincere and were given a garden called al-Hayawan, whose single cluster could be carried by a mule, a report that several commentators repeat. Al-Hasan however doubts their faith, while most hold that they repented. Several exegetes then apply the story to the Quraysh, who were tested by famine and urged to repent, and conclude that the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew.

This passage recounts what the people of the garden said when they found their orchard destroyed. Regretting their plan to deny the poor their share and their failure to say "God willing" in their oath, they cried out: "Woe to us! We were indeed transgressors." Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand "tughat" as disobedience and withholding the rights of the poor, while Ibn Kaysan takes it as ingratitude for God's blessings. Their hope that their Lord would give them something better is generally read as sincere repentance and a request for pardon; Ibn Mas'ud reports that they were rewarded with a garden whose grapes were enormous. Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari and most commentators apply the story to the Quraysh: the worldly punishment is like that of the garden, but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater. Scholars differ on the meaning of "tusabbihun": Ibn Jurayj and the majority take it to mean the exception "if God wills"; Abu Salih takes it as the phrase "glory be to God"; Mujahid and al-Zamakhshari see it as glorifying God by acknowledging His will. Al-Hasan doubts that these people were believers, whereas most hold that they repented and were sincere.

This verse records the words of the owners of the garden, who, after their orchard was destroyed in the night, regretted having denied the poor their share, confessed their wrongdoing and rebellion, and then hoped that their Lord would give them something better in its place, since they turned back to Him. Al-Tabari explains that they repented of their fault in failing to make the exception of God's will, and that their hope is tied to that repentance. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy mention two possibilities: a better replacement in this world or a reward in the next, with Ibn Juzayy preferring the first on the basis of a report from Ibn Mas'ud. Most commentators, including al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud, hold that they truly repented and were sincere, and they cite Ibn Mas'ud's report that God gave them a garden called al-Hayawan, whose single cluster of grapes was carried by a mule. Al-Hasan, however, withheld judgement on their faith, not knowing whether their words expressed true belief or were the cry of distress that unbelievers utter in hardship. Al-Razi likewise notes that the words may express a desire for worldly gain rather than repentance. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the story a lesson for the Quraysh, who are urged to turn quickly back to God and acknowledge their ingratitude. Abu Hayyan records that the readers differ on whether the verb yubdilana is doubled, while the meaning remains the same.

This verse closes the story of the owners of the garden. In its plain sense, as most commentators explain it, « such is the punishment » refers to the punishment of this world, the ruin of the garden, and the punishment of the Hereafter is far greater, if only they knew. Al-Tabari, Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Zayd tie the worldly punishment to the destruction that struck those who disobeyed God's command, and read the closing phrase as a rebuke of those who do not know. Al-Tabari adds that if the idolaters knew how much greater God's punishment of polytheists is in the Hereafter, they would hold back and repent. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn Sa'di and the Jalalayn read the verse as a general rule: whoever withholds what God has given and opposes His command receives a similar punishment in this life and a greater one in the next.

The commentators differ on who the warning is addressed to. Ibn Abbas, al-Samani and al-Jaza'iri apply it to the Meccan unbelievers, and al-Samani recalls their defeat at Badr. Ibn Ashur explains that « they » are the idolaters who deny the Hereafter, and that the comparison concerns the kind of punishment rather than its degree. Al-Qurtubi finds the Badr reading hard to sustain because the surah is Meccan, and notes that others apply the verse to the famine that struck Quraysh. All agree that the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, while they differ over the intended audience.

This verse states that those who are mindful of God, by performing their duties and avoiding what He forbids, will have with their Lord in the Hereafter gardens of pure bliss, free from any disturbance or fear of loss, unlike the gardens of this world, as al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud explain. The commentators agree that it follows the story of the people of the garden in Surah al-Qalam and contrasts the fate of the righteous with that of the wicked. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report that the following verses answer the Quraysh, who claimed that if such gardens existed they would have the greater share; the reply takes the form of a rebuke: shall We treat the Muslims like the criminals? Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada understand the zaʿim as the guarantor, while al-Hasan takes it to mean the Messenger. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya stress that these questions are reproaches: the disbelievers have no book, covenant or partners to support their claims. Regarding the uncovering of the shin on the Day of Judgment, most read it as an image of the severity of that day, supported by Arabic verse, while others relate it to a divine attribute as reported in hadith. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani holds that the threat concerns the polytheists in this world, but al-Razi replies that prostration in the Hereafter is a rebuke rather than an obligation.

This verse is a rhetorical rebuke: God declares it unthinkable that He would treat the believers who submit to Him the same as the wrongdoers. Al-Tabari explains that the God-fearing, who obey their Lord and avoid what He forbids, will have gardens of lasting bliss, and that equating the obedient with the disobedient in honour is unacceptable. Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn read it the same way: the two groups are not equal in reward. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Shawkani link the verse to the Quraysh, who claimed that if they were raised again their state would be better than that of the Muslims, as it had been in this world, and the verse answers that claim. Az-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya take the address to be to the polytheists, shifted into the second person, and see the question 'What is wrong with you, how do you judge?' as a mockery of their crooked reasoning. Al-Razi adds that the verse denies equality in reward and not the possibility that one person could be both a believer and a sinner, and he answers al-Qadi, who had drawn that conclusion from it. On the sense of 'the guilty', Ibn Juzayy, al-Nasafi and al-Shawkani identify them as the disbelievers, while al-Razi allows a wider meaning. The commentators also discuss the grammar of the following clauses and the readings of the word 'that' in the phrase 'that for you'.

This verse, as the commentators explain it, states that it is unthinkable to treat those who obey God the same as the wrongdoers, and that such a judgment is crooked and could not come from a sound mind. Al-Tabari, al-Sam'ani, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi read it as a rebuke to the Quraysh, who claimed that they would have in the Hereafter an equal or better share than the believers, the question being rhetorical and disapproving.

Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi explain that the judgment of recompense has not been handed over to people so that they may decide as they wish. Al-Razi examines the meaning of likeness: in his view the denial concerns equality in reward rather than resemblance in every respect, and he notes that the criminals here may refer to the particular unbelievers mentioned in the account. He does not settle whether a sinner may enter Paradise.

The commentators agree that the verses that follow demand a book, a binding oath, a guarantor or partners, in order to refute every claim. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Qurtubi explain the verb "study" as "read", and the vowelling of the particle "inna" after the phrase "in it you find", without any of them preferring one reading over another in this context.

Ibn Kathir holds that the verse affirms that those who obey God are not like those who disobey him in reward, and that the opposite judgment is false. Ibn 'Ashur specifies that the reproach targets the polytheists who thought they had an advantage in the Hereafter as they had in this world. Al-Biqa'i and al-Shawkani stress the ignorance of those who claim this and the falseness of their opinion, without going into legal details.

This verse follows God's rebuke of the Meccan disbelievers, who claimed that in the afterlife they would receive better than the believers. It asks them whether they have a Book in which they study that they will have whatever they choose. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy take tadrusun to mean reading or memorizing a scripture sent down from heaven, and Ibn Zayd identifies it with the revelation they claim to recite. Al-Sam'ani gives a second sense, that they study and closely examine a matter so as to pass judgment from it themselves. The commentators agree that the question is one of mockery and denial, since they have no such proof. On grammar, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy explain that the clause introduced by inna is the object of tadrusun, and its initial hamza takes a kasra because of the lam that follows it; al-Zamakhshari also allows that it may be a direct quotation of what is studied, as in the Sura of the Ranks. Abu Hayyan notes that Talha and al-Dahhak read it with a fatha. Ibn Ashur sees the verse moving from rebuke to argument, asking what grounds their judgment: a Book, a covenant from God, a guarantor, or partners. None of these is available to them.

This verse rebukes the idolaters who claimed that in the Hereafter they would receive better than the believers. God rejects their claim by denying that Muslims should be treated like criminals. The commentators explain that He asks them whether they possess a Book from God in which they read that they will get whatever they choose. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir see this as a rebuke and a reproach for their false wishes. The exegetes agree on the general sense: if they have such a proof, let them produce it.

The commentators also discuss the grammar of the phrase "inna lakum". According to al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Nasafi, the particle was originally opened and became broken because of the lam, and the clause may be a quotation of what is studied. Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud explain that "takhayyarun" means choosing for oneself and desiring. Some readers took the form as a question, which Abu Hayyan notes.

On the phrase "bāligha" describing the oaths, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand emphatic and absolute oaths, while al-Mawardi offers another reading, that God pledged not to punish them in this world until the Day of Resurrection. Regarding "za'im", Ibn Abbas and Qatada take it as guarantor, al-Hasan as the Messenger, and Ibn Kaysan as the one who upholds the argument. The commentators conclude that without a book, a covenant, a guarantor or partners, their claim has no basis.

Al-Zamakhshari links this passage to the debate about the rewards of the Hereafter, in the context of the surah and the story of the people of the garden.

The commentators explain that this verse addresses the leaders of Quraysh who claimed that they would receive in the afterlife as much as, or more than, the believers. The reply takes the form of a rebuke in the shape of a question: do you hold binding oaths from Us, reaching to the Day of Resurrection, that you shall have whatever you decide for yourselves? Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the word balighah to mean firm and emphatic, and see the clause that follows as the answer to the oath. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan explain that the sentence amounts to asking whether God has sworn such an oath in their favour. Abu Hayyan also records a reading attributed to al-Hasan with the accusative, used as a circumstantial state.

The commentators agree that this claim has no basis: there is no scripture that supports it, no covenant from God, and no associates or witnesses to confirm it. This is why the verse goes on to say, ask them which of them stands surety for it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the surety (za'im) as a guarantor or spokesman; Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada take it as a bail-giver, al-Hasan as the Messenger, and Ibn Kaysan as one who maintains the argument. As for the associates, most identify them as idols, while others take them to be witnesses who would vouch for their claims.

The next verse, speaking of the day when a shin is uncovered, is read by most commentators as a day of extreme severity. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Baghawi explain it as a figure for the gravity of the ordeal, while al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan cite hadiths describing the uncovering of the shin on the Day of Judgement. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, however, takes it as a threat in this world rather than the next, a view al-Razi discusses. The precise meaning, these scholars note, rests with God.

God instructs His Messenger to ask the disbelievers which of them stands surety for their claim that they will receive in the Hereafter something better than what the believers receive, a rebuke of this false judgment. Most commentators understand za'im as a guarantor or surety, while Ibn Kaysan takes it to mean one who upholds the argument and the claim, and al-Hasan takes it to mean the Messenger. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, followed by al-Tabari, read it as the one who takes responsibility for this claim. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya see the verse as denying them any support, rational or scriptural, for their position. It implies they have no revealed book, no covenant from God, no guarantor and no partners who would confirm their words. Al-Mawardi and al-Tabari report that the partners may be the idols or witnesses who would attest to their claim. Most commentators link this passage to the scene that follows, the day when a shin will be uncovered, and understand it as the Day of Resurrection, whereas Abu Muslim al-Isfahani reads it as a worldly threat. Al-Razi holds that the command to prostrate on that day is a rebuke rather than a binding obligation. Several exegetes leave the choice between these readings open.

This passage of Surah al-Qalam rebukes the disbelievers for claiming that they will receive in the Hereafter what the Muslims receive, or more. The commentators explain that the verse 'Or do they have associates? Let them bring their associates, if they are truthful' denies that they have any partners who would agree with their claim or testify for them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the za'im as the guarantor of this claim, and the associates as lords who would act so or witnesses who would confirm their truthfulness. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada take the za'im to be the surety, al-Hasan takes him to be the Messenger, and Ibn Kaysan takes him to be the one who upholds the argument. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy hold that the associates are people who share their view, though Ibn Juzayy considers the reading of idols more apparent. Abu Hayyan and al-Shawkani note that the command 'let them bring' is a challenge, and most exegetes take the associates to be idols. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the criminals may refer to the disbelievers already mentioned. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir explain the 'day when the leg is uncovered' as the most terrible moment of the Day of Judgment, while al-Alusi and others report the literal narration, which Ibn Hazm defends. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani reads it as a worldly threat. All agree that the disbelievers' claim is baseless, since they have neither a book, a divine pledge, nor any supporter.

This verse describes the Day of Judgment, when the matter becomes so terrible that the shin is uncovered, an image which, according to most commentators, means the extreme severity of the ordeal. The Arabs used to say that a man who buckled down to a serious task would roll up his garment to the shin, and the phrase was extended to mean any hard event. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, citing Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, take it to mean the greatest distress and the most dreadful hour of the Day. Al-Mawardi also gives the senses of a veil being lifted and the arrival of the Hereafter, and Ibn Ashur reads it as a picture of intense anguish. Several scholars cite reports in the two Sahihs in which God uncovers His shin, the believers prostrate, and the hypocrites cannot. Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Shawkani treat these as support for the literal reading, which Ibn Kathir reports without deciding. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi regard the phrase as a metaphor and reject a literal shin, while Ibn Sa'di and al-Qasimi accept the reports with caution. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani places the verse at the moment of death, a view Razi discusses. On prostration, the commentators agree it is a rebuke rather than an obligation, since the Hereafter is no place for worship. They also agree that unbelievers and hypocrites cannot prostrate, their backs becoming one solid bone. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi connect this to those who ignored the call to prayer in this world, a point al-Jaza'iri and Ibn Juzayy also make. Finally, God tells His Prophet to leave the deniers to Him and to be patient.

This verse describes the state of the wrongdoers on the Day of Resurrection: when the shin is uncovered, they will be called to prostrate and will be unable to do so, their gaze lowered and humiliation covering them. In the world they had been called to prostration while healthy and able, yet they refused. The commentators broadly agree that the uncovering of the shin describes the extreme severity of that day. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada that it means a terrible event, citing the Arabic idiom that war has bared its shin. As for the call to prostrate, Ibrahim al-Taymi and al-Sha'bi understood it as the obligatory prayer, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said they heard the call 'hasten to success' and did not respond. Ka'b al-Ahbar held that the verse was revealed about those who stay away from congregational prayer. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani argued that the verse refers to a worldly threat rather than the afterlife, since there is no duty in the hereafter; al-Razi replied that the call then serves as rebuke rather than obligation. Al-Zamakhshari treated the uncovering of the shin as a pure metaphor, while others took it as a great light or a veil being lifted. On the meaning of istidraj, al-Hasan saw it as a kindness that deceives its recipient, al-Thawri as blessings granted while gratitude is forgotten, and Ibn Kathir as an apparent honour that is in reality a humiliation.

The commentators explain that God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to leave the matter of those who deny the Quran to Him, for He will deal with them, which is both a consolation to the Prophet and a warning to the deniers. For most, istidraj means leading a person step by step toward ruin: his blessings are increased, and he takes them as a favour when they are in fact the cause of his destruction. Imla is the granting of respite and the lengthening of time, and kayd here means the punishment that will befall them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that God grants them respite in this life so that the proof against them may be complete. Abu Hayyan, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Su'ud note that they take these favours as a sign of preference over the believers, while these favours lead them to ruin. Most identify the hadith with the Quran, though Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan mention the possibility that it refers to the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain istidraj as successive blessings and the forgetting of gratitude. Al-Razi reports that some scholars held this part of the verse abrogated by the verse of the sword, an opinion the others do not adopt. Al-Hasan al-Basri's saying that many are led astray by the kindness shown to them is widely cited. Ibn 'Ashur explains that istidraj leads to punishment through causes that people do not perceive.

The commentators explain that God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to leave to Him those who deny the Quran, for He will deal with them and requite them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi understand that God will lead them step by step, little by little, to the place they do not know, through blessings they take as good fortune but which bring about their ruin, and that 'I give them respite' means He lengthens their time. There is broad agreement that what appears as a favour is in fact a snare, and that the word 'scheme' (kayd) is used because the favour takes the form of a scheme, while 'firm' (matin) describes the strength of its effect in bringing about destruction. Al-Zamakhshari notes that health, provision and long life are blessings that ought to lead to gratitude, but the disbelievers make them a cause of unbelief by their own choice. Al-Hasan al-Basri says that many are led on by kindness, deceived by praise or by being covered over. Sufyan al-Thawri adds that God lavishes blessings and makes them forget thankfulness, while Abu Rawq says that every sin is followed by a new blessing. Al-Ka'bi understands the leading on to refer to death, which comes without people knowing its time, whereas al-Jubba'i takes it to mean punishment in the Hereafter. The commentators present these views side by side without deciding between them. Their common conclusion is that the respite serves to complete the proof against the disbelievers, so that whoever is destroyed is destroyed with clear evidence.

In this verse God affirms that the Prophet ﷺ did not ask the idolaters for any worldly wage in return for conveying the message, so the weight of a financial burden cannot be the reason for their refusal. Al-Tabari, al-Nasafi, and Ibn Juzayy read the interrogative as a rebuke and a negation rather than an affirmation. Al-Tabari explains that the disbelievers shunned accepting the counsel because of the heavy burden of what would be asked of them. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, and al-Qurtubi give the same sense: maghram means a financial levy that would weigh on them and deter them from faith. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as refuting the last excuse that those who turn away might invoke, namely the financial cost. Al-Shinqiti specifies that the wage denied is material gain, citing the verse: say, I ask you for no reward except affection for my kin. Ibn Sa'di stresses that the call was solely for the good of the listeners, without demanding their wealth. The commentators agree on the context of rebuking the disbelievers and differ on some grammatical points without choosing between them. The following phrase about the unseen knowledge is read as showing that the disbelievers have no proof for their claims.

This verse rebukes the disbelievers with a rhetorical question: do they possess knowledge of the unseen, so that they can write down for themselves what they claim? Most commentators, including Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud, understand the unseen to be the Preserved Tablet, from which they could read what is to come. Al-Tabari adds that the disbelievers used this supposed knowledge to dispute with the Prophet and to claim that, despite their disbelief, they were held in higher esteem by God than the believers. Al-Razi gives two readings: either the Tablet records the reward of their disbelief, which makes them persist in it, or the hidden matters seem present to their minds, so that they pass judgment on God as they wish. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur take the verb "write" to mean decree or prescribe: they set their own rules and impose them on their followers. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the knowledge of the unseen has been claimed by their leaders rather than by God. Ibn Kathir and other commentators connect the verse to its context, which dismisses the disbelievers' excuses: God asks them for no wage that could burden them, and they have no knowledge that could justify their refusal. Ibn Sa'di notes that in such a situation the Prophet is left with only patience.

In this verse God commands His Prophet ﷺ to be patient with the decree of his Lord, which most commentators take to mean accepting the delay granted to the disbelievers and the postponement of his victory over them. He is also told not to be like the companion of the fish, Yunus (Jonah), who called out from inside the fish while he was distressed, or 'maktum', filled with grief. The commentators generally agree that the prohibition concerns the state that led Yunus to that ordeal, namely his anger at his people and his lack of patience, rather than the supplication itself, for which God praised him. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi cite his words: 'There is no god but You, glory be to You, I was among the wrongdoers.' Scholars differ on the meaning of 'maktum': Ibn Abbas and Mujahid say grieved, Ata' and Abu Malik say distressed, al-Mawardi says confined, and al-Mubarrad says seized by the throat. Qatada reads the verse as a warning against haste and anger, while al-Tabari takes it to mean weakness in conveying the message. On the 'blessing of God' that rescued him, opinions vary: prophethood according to al-Dahhak, his earlier worship according to Ibn Jubayr, his supplication according to Ibn Zayd, and his release from the fish according to Ibn Bahr. Being cast out 'in the open wasteland' means being left in an empty plain, and 'blameworthy' is understood as sinful by some and as deserving reproach by others. Most commentators explain the verse about the 'gaze that would make you slip' as a hostile, envious stare, while others see it as the evil eye, a belief known among the Arabs, and al-Hasan recommends reciting this passage as a remedy against it.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the command to the Prophet ﷺ to be patient with his Lord's decree, including the delay of his enemies' punishment and the postponement of his victory, and the warning not to be like the companion of the fish, Yunus, in impatience and haste. Their reading is that had a blessing from his Lord not overtaken Yunus, he would have been cast out onto a bare open land while blameworthy. Because he was shown mercy, he was cast out while not blameworthy.

There is broad agreement on the meaning of key terms. Al-'arā' is an open, bare land without buildings or trees, and al-makzūm is one filled with grief. Most take the blessing to be God granting him repentance and accepting it. Ibn 'Abbas explains madhmūm as blameworthy, Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah as sinful, and Ibn Juzayy and others as one cut off from all good.

The scholars differ on which blessing is meant. Al-Dahhak says prophethood, Ibn Jubayr his earlier worship, Ibn Zayd his cry, 'There is no god but You, glory be to You, I was among the wrongdoers', and Ibn Bahr his rescue from the fish's belly. On the place of exposure, al-Mawardi and al-Tabari take it to be the open ground or the gathering place of Judgment Day, and al-Alusi finds the latter very remote. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan hold that the negation concerns the blame rather than the casting out, a view also held by Ibn 'Atiyya. Ibn 'Ashur reads the verse as a warning to the Prophet against falling into a distress like Yunus's.

The commentators explain that this verse says God chose Yunus after His mercy and his repentance reached him, and made him one of the righteous, meaning the prophets and messengers. Ibn 'Abbas and others report that God returned revelation to him and interceded for him with his people. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and several others hold that this choosing may mean his sending as a messenger after a time when he was not yet one, while Abu al-Su'ud notes that he was sent to a hundred thousand people or more. Al-Nasafi and others explain that righteousness here means moral completeness, God having preserved him from any act that would have been better avoided. Al-Nasafi takes the righteous to be prophets, and most hold that he was already a messenger before, as the verses of the Rank sura suggest. All agree that choosing means selection. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur link the passage to a warning against haste and impatience, Ibn 'Ashur seeing in it an exhortation to the Prophet to persevere in carrying out God's command. The commentaries draw no legal ruling here and focus on the lesson of Yunus's story and his standing before God.

This verse describes how the disbelievers, in their intense hostility toward the Prophet ﷺ, almost made him stumble or perished through their piercing, hateful glances as they heard the Qur'an, while still calling him mad. The commentators agree that the glances express extreme hatred and envy. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the verb is read with a damma on the ya (from azlaqa) or a fatha (from zalaqa), two readings that they regard as close in meaning, and al-Tabari does not prefer one over the other. As to the meaning, al-Kalbi, al-Mawardi, al-Sam'ani, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi relate the belief in the evil eye, recounting that a man from the tribe of Banu Asad would fast three days and then strike with his eye whatever pleased him. Ibn Qutayba, al-Zajjaj and al-Qushayri hold instead that the glance was one of hatred, not admiration, since the evil eye requires approval. Ibn al-Qayyim reconciles both views by observing that a hostile glance can also have an effect. Al-Hasan reports that reciting this verse is a remedy for the evil eye. Most commentators conclude that the Qur'an is a reminder to the worlds, which answers the charge of madness.

This verse states that the Quran is nothing but a reminder and an admonition for all the worlds, meaning humans and jinn, and it closes the rebuttal of the claim that the Prophet ﷺ was mad. The commentators offer two main readings. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi, Qatada and Ibn Kathir understand the reminder to be the Quran itself, an admonition to believers and a recalling of promise and threat. Al-Mawardi, al-Sam'ani, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Jawzi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Shawkani explain that it may also mean a nobility for the worlds, citing the verse that the Quran is a reminder for you and your people. Al-Sam'ani holds that the more apparent reading makes the Quran the reminder, while others take the Prophet himself to be the reminder. Al-Qurtubi keeps both possibilities open. All agree on the force of the rebuttal: one who brings such a message cannot be insane. Most take 'the worlds' to mean jinn and humans, though al-Mawardi notes it may include every created nation. The commentators do not choose between these readings and present them as compatible with the context of the surah.
